intro: In this final college you'll learn how to talk about television and the programmes you watched, social media, the news and current events, and how to give your opinion about all of it in Dutch.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome to the final theme
paragraphs.text: Welcome to the very last theme of your course. Its title is [[Waar gaat het over?]], which means 'what's it about?'. You will hear that question all the time, because Dutch people love to chat about television, the news, and what people share online. Imagine you are at work or at the coffee machine, and a colleague asks [[Heb je dat gezien?]], meaning 'did you see that?'. To join in, you need a few key words. The news is [[het nieuws]], a newspaper is [[de krant]], and a TV programme is [[het programma]]. Television itself is [[de televisie]], usually shortened to [[de tv]]. A channel is [[de zender]], and one episode of a series is [[de aflevering]]. When something is in the news, you might say [[Dat was in het nieuws]], which means 'that was in the news'. In this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word and sentence is spoken by a native voice, so listen closely and repeat each phrase out loud. This is the perfect theme to finish on, because talking about media is how you make real friends here. So get comfortable, and [[laten we beginnen!]] — let's begin!

paragraphs.heading: Did you see that? The perfect tense
paragraphs.text: To talk about what you watched or heard, Dutch uses the perfect tense. You take a form of the verb [[hebben]], which means 'to have', and you put a special past-participle word at the very end of the sentence. The most useful one here is [[gezien]], 'seen'. So a colleague asks [[Heb je dat gezien?]], 'did you see that?', and you answer [[Ja, ik heb het gezien.]], 'yes, I saw it'. For reading, the participle is [[gelezen]]. If you read the news online, you say [[Ik heb het gelezen]], which means 'I read it'. For hearing, it is [[gehoord]], so you can ask [[Heb je daar iets over gehoord?]], 'have you heard anything about that?'. And for watching a programme on purpose, the participle is [[gekeken]], as in [[We hebben gisteren het journaal gekeken.]], 'we watched the TV news yesterday'. Notice that little word [[al]], which means 'yet' or 'already'. A very natural question is [[Heb je het al gezien?]], 'have you seen it yet?'. To say 'not yet', you answer [[Nee, nog niet.]]. Practise these four participles — [[gezien]], [[gelezen]], [[gehoord]], [[gekeken]] — because they unlock dozens of everyday conversations.

paragraphs.heading: Talking about TV and programmes
paragraphs.text: Now let's talk about watching television, which the Dutch do a lot. To say you watch something, you use the verb [[kijken]] with the little word [[naar]], meaning 'to watch'. So you say [[Ik kijk naar het journaal.]], 'I watch the TV news'. That word [[het journaal]] is important: it is the official daily TV news on the public channels, and the big evening edition at eight o'clock is famous all over the country. A talkshow is simply [[een talkshow]], and in the evening many people watch one to hear guests discuss the day's events. To ask a friend what a programme is about, you say [[Waar gaat dit programma over?]]. To ask their opinion, you say [[Wat vind jij van dit programma?]], 'what do you think of this programme?'. One thing everybody complains about is the advertising, [[de reclame]]. You will often hear [[Er is te veel reclame op tv.]], 'there is too much advertising on TV'. If you love a series, you can say [[Ik kijk elke week naar een nieuwe aflevering.]], 'I watch a new episode every week'. And the people watching at home are [[de kijkers]], 'the viewers' — a word the presenters use to greet you.

paragraphs.heading: Social media and the news
paragraphs.text: These days a lot of news arrives through your phone, on social media, which in Dutch is [[sociale media]]. A short video clip is [[het filmpje]], a lovely little word you will use often. To say you saw a funny video, you say [[Ik heb een grappig filmpje gezien.]]. An online account is [[het account]], and to follow one you use the verb [[volgen]]: [[Ik volg dat account.]], 'I follow that account'. To share something, the verb is [[delen]], so you might ask [[Heb je dit filmpje al gedeeld?]], 'have you shared this video yet?'. Many people read the news on their phone — a hugely popular Dutch news website is called NU.nl. You can say [[Ik lees het nieuws meestal online.]], 'I usually read the news online'. A single news item or message is [[het bericht]], and the topic of a story is [[het onderwerp]]. To ask what a story is about, you say [[Waar gaat het bericht over?]]. When something is everywhere in the press, the Dutch say [[Het staat in alle kranten.]], 'it's in all the newspapers'. So whether it reaches you on paper, on tv, or on your phone, you now have the words to talk about it.

paragraphs.heading: Giving your opinion
paragraphs.text: Talking about the news is only half the fun — the other half is saying what you think. The key phrase is [[Ik vind]], which means 'I find' or 'I think'. You can say [[Ik vind het nieuws vaak te negatief.]], 'I find the news often too negative'. To give a full opinion, use [[Ik vind dat]] and then a little sentence, but watch out: after [[dat]] the verb jumps to the end. So you say [[Ik vind dat er te veel reclame op tv is.]], 'I think there is too much advertising on TV'. Another lovely opener is [[Volgens mij]], which means 'in my opinion' or 'I think', as in [[Volgens mij is dat niet waar.]], 'I don't think that's true'. To ask someone else, say [[Wat vind jij ervan?]], 'what do you think of it?'. And to react, learn these whole phrases: to agree, [[Ik ben het met je eens.]], 'I agree with you', or simply [[Je hebt gelijk.]], 'you're right'. To agree about something, [[Daar ben ik het mee eens.]]. To disagree gently, [[Daar ben ik het niet mee eens.]], 'I don't agree with that'. Now you can have a real discussion!

paragraphs.heading: Putting it together — and well done!
paragraphs.text: Let's put it all together. Imagine you meet your neighbour outside. You ask [[Heb je het journaal van gisteren gezien?]], 'did you see yesterday's TV news?'. She says [[Nee, nog niet. Waar gaat het over?]], 'no, not yet, what's it about?'. You explain [[Het ging over het weer; het wordt heel warm.]], 'it was about the weather; it's going to be very warm'. She replies [[O, dat heb ik wel op sociale media gezien.]], 'oh, I did see that on social media'. You add your opinion: [[Ik vind dat er te veel slecht nieuws is.]], and she agrees warmly: [[Daar ben ik het helemaal mee eens.]]. That little chat uses everything from this theme. And now, something special: this was the final theme of your whole course. You have travelled from saying your name all the way to discussing the news and sharing your opinion — that is a huge achievement. Be proud of every Dutch word you can now say. Keep listening, keep reading [[de krant]], keep watching [[het journaal]], and keep talking with the people around you. From the bottom of my heart: [[Gefeliciteerd!]] — congratulations! [[Je hebt het fantastisch gedaan. Heel veel succes in Nederland!]]
